cards: Dorothy Garrod excavates Shuqba Cave and finds a layer of microliths between Upper Palaeolithic and Bronze Age deposits
After finding similar material at el-Wad, Garrod names the Natufian culture after the Wadi Natuf
Residues of 13,000-year-old beer are reported from a cave near Haifa
A survey directed by Halet Çambel and Robert John Braidwood first noted the site
Klaus Schmidt began excavations and soon unearthed the first of the T-shaped pillars
UNESCO designated Göbekli Tepe a World Heritage Site
Herod begins to rule Judea and later greatly expands the royal domain at Jericho
A Christian pilgrim describes Jericho, and soon afterwards the Byzantine town is built to the east
The Ayyubid forces of Saladin evict the Crusaders
Administrative control of Jericho passes to the Palestinian Authority
Henry Hall begins the first large excavation of Ubaid material at Tell al-ʿUbaid
A conference in Baghdad defines the ‘Ubaid pottery style’
Joan Oates shows that the Eridu and Hajji Muhammed styles belong to the Ubaid and divides it into phases
Ashur-uballit I reclaims the city from Mitanni and founds the Middle Assyrian Empire
A coalition of Babylonians, Medes and Scythians sacks and razes the city
Nineveh is a bishopric of the Church of the East
The Arabs conquer the area and build a mosque on the west bank
Benjamin of Tudela visits the site
Columbus reaches the Taíno chiefdoms of the Caribbean; Spanish conquest destroys them within a generation
Hernando de Soto’s expedition passes through Cofitachequi and Coosa, paramount chiefdoms of the South-East
English colonists at Jamestown meet Wahunsenacawh, paramount chief of some thirty peoples of Tidewater Virginia
Kamehameha I conquers Oʻahu at the Battle of Nuʻuanu; by 1810 he rules all the Hawaiian Islands
Kalervo Oberg names the chiefdom as a type; Elman Service sets it between tribe and state in 1962
Ashurbanipal of Assyria levels the city
Cyrus the Great takes Susa, which becomes part of the Achaemenid Empire
Shapur II destroys the city after a rebellion of its Christians
An Arab army under Abu Musa al-Ash'ari captures Susa
Philip II of Macedon defeats Athens and Thebes at Chaeronea and takes control of mainland Greece
Tikal is defeated by Caracol, an ally of Calakmul, in the wars of the Classic Maya city-states
The Lombard League of Italian communes defeats Emperor Frederick Barbarossa at the Battle of Legnano
The Treaty of Stralsund ends the Hanseatic towns’ war with Denmark at the height of the league’s power
A Portuguese fleet sacks Kilwa and Mombasa, leading city-states of the Swahili coast
Singapore leaves the Federation of Malaysia and becomes an independent city-state
The Achaemenid Empire of Cyrus the Great conquers Mesopotamia but leaves its native religion undisturbed
The scholar Jules Oppert gives the rediscovered language the name Sumerian
A statue of King Ibbit-Lim identifies Tell Mardikh as Ebla
First settlement is established near the Gihon Spring, according to archaeological evidence
The Neo-Babylonian Empire captures Jerusalem and burns the Temple
Judas Maccabeus captures Jerusalem and restores temple worship
Titus destroys much of Jerusalem and the Second Temple after a five-month siege
Jerusalem is conquered by the Rashidun Caliphate
The Crusaders take Jerusalem and make it capital of the Kingdom of Jerusalem
Israel takes East Jerusalem in the Six-Day War
Bedouin find a statue on Tell Hariri, leading to French excavations
Humban-nikash I fights Sargon II of Assyria at the Battle of Der
Sennacherib's son Ashur-nadin-shumi is handed to Elam and dies in captivity
Byblos passes under the Achaemenid Empire
Byblos submits to Alexander the Great and its king joins the siege of Tyre
Cyrus the Great takes Babylon and records his conquest in Akkadian on the Cyrus Cylinder
Four scholars independently translate an Assyrian inscription, proving the decipherment
The Chicago Assyrian Dictionary is completed after nearly ninety years of work
Hammurabi becomes king and builds Babylon into the capital of southern Mesopotamia
The city is thought to have been sacked by the Hittite king Mursili I
Sennacherib of Assyria destroys the city
Cyrus the Great takes Babylon and ends the Neo-Babylonian Empire
Alexander the Great enters Babylon after the Battle of Gaugamela
Robert Koldewey begins the first scientific excavations
UNESCO inscribes Babylon as a World Heritage Site
King Uperi of Dilmun sends gifts to Sargon II of Assyria
Dilmun passes with Babylonia to the Achaemenid Empire
Danish expedition under P.V. Glob and Geoffrey Bibby begins excavations
Adad-nirari II launches the Neo-Assyrian revival
Tiglath-pileser III takes the throne and reorganises army and provinces
Samaria falls and the population of the Kingdom of Israel is deported
Esarhaddon conquers Egypt, bringing the empire to its greatest extent
Babylonians and Medes destroy the Assyrian capital Nineveh
Ashur-uballit II fails to retake Harran and vanishes from the record
The Temple of Bel is dedicated
Hadrian visits, names the city Hadriane Palmyra and makes it a free city
Odaenathus defeats Shapur I near the Euphrates and becomes the ruler of a de facto allied kingdom
Aurelian razes the city after a rebellion
The Rashidun Caliphate takes the city under Khalid ibn al-Walid
Timur attacks and destroys the city, reducing it to a small village
The villagers are moved to the new village of Tadmur and the ancient site is opened to excavation
Hammurabi defeats an Elamite-led coalition, launching his conquests
Hammurabi conquers Larsa, bringing all southern Mesopotamia under his rule
Hammurabi conquers his former ally Mari
Hammurabi dies; his son Samsu-iluna soon faces widespread revolt
Samsi-Addu dies and his Kingdom of Upper Mesopotamia disintegrates; in the struggle that follows Hammurabi allies with Zimri-Lim of Mari
With the help of Zimri-Lim he takes Larsa, brings out its king Rim-Sin alive and annexes the kingdom, gaining the whole lower Mesopotamian plain
Hormuzd Rassam finds the Standard Babylonian version in the ruins of the library of Ashurbanipal
George Smith reads translated fragments of the epic before the Society of Biblical Archaeology
Andrew George publishes his two-volume critical edition with Oxford University Press
The Gilgamesh Dream Tablet, seized by US officials in 2019, is returned to Iraq
Ugaritic troops fight for the Hittites at the Battle of Kadesh
A farmer’s discovery of a tomb at Minet el-Beida leads to excavations
Claude Schaeffer begins excavating Ras Shamra
Jean-Vincent Scheil publishes the editio princeps, with a transliteration and a free translation into French
Benno Landsberger begins the line of criticism that most judges paid the Code no attention, against the view that it was enforced law
Muwatalli II fights Ramesses II at Kadesh, perhaps the largest chariot battle of antiquity
Sidon's navy plays a significant role at the Battle of Salamis, aligned with the Persian fleet against the Greeks.
Artaxerxes III invades Phoenicia at the end of the Persian era.
Alexander the Great occupies Sidon, beginning its Hellenistic period.
Ramesses II leaves Pi-Ramesses with four divisions and marches along the coast through Gaza
Two Shasu nomads give Ramesses a false report that the Hittites are far off at Aleppo
Hittite chariots cross the Orontes, scatter the Re division and attack the Egyptian camp
An Egyptian counterattack, the arrival of the Ne'arin and the Ptah division drive the Hittites back to the river
Ramesses II and Hattusili III make a peace treaty in the 21st year of Ramesses' reign
An eclipse ends the war with Media; the Halys becomes the frontier
Tyrians traditionally found Carthage, as settlements spread to Cyprus, Sicily, Sardinia and Spain
Esarhaddon of Assyria captures rebellious Sidon and deports its people
The cities pass under Persian rule; their ships form the core of the Persian navy
Alexander the Great takes Tyre after a siege of about seven months
Ardashir I founds the Sasanian Empire, under which Zoroastrianism becomes the state religion
The last Sasanian king, Yazdegerd III, is killed after the Arab conquest of Iran
The Parsi Dadabhai Naoroji becomes the first Asian elected to the British House of Commons
Jean-Jacques Barthélemy deciphers the alphabet from the Cippi of Melqart, a Greek and Punic bilingual
The Sasanian era begins, the period in which the Avestan alphabet is created and the Avesta first written down
The oldest surviving fragment of an Avestan manuscript, known as K1, is dated to this year
Abraham Hyacinthe Anquetil-Duperron travels to India and finds the texts among the Parsi communities
Westergaard publishes the first critical edition of the Avesta
An Assyrian inscription makes the last unambiguous reference to Edom
Eliezer Ben-Yehuda settles in Jerusalem and begins his campaign to revive spoken Hebrew
The British Mandate for Palestine recognises Hebrew as an official language beside English and Arabic
The first Dead Sea Scrolls, including the oldest known manuscripts of the Hebrew Bible, are found near Qumran
Israel founds the Academy of the Hebrew Language
The Babylonians destroy Jerusalem and the First Temple and take many Judeans into exile
The Second Temple is completed in Jerusalem after the return from exile, by the traditional date
The Romans destroy Jerusalem and the Second Temple at the end of the Jewish revolt
The Jews are expelled from Spain
The State of Israel is founded, three years after the end of the Holocaust
The Cypress of Kashmar, said to have been planted by Zoroaster, is felled on the order of al-Mutawakkil
Ahab fights Shalmaneser III of Assyria at the Battle of Qarqar
Tiglath-pileser III annexes Galilee and Gilead
Samaria falls to the Assyrians after a long siege
Sargon II deports some 27,000 people and creates the province of Samerina
Sennacherib invades Judah, takes Lachish and besieges Jerusalem
Josiah’s religious reform centralises worship in Jerusalem
Josiah is killed at Megiddo confronting the pharaoh Necho II
Nebuchadnezzar II captures Jerusalem and deports Jehoiachin
Jerusalem and the temple are destroyed; the elite are exiled to Babylon
The advance of the Islamic State drives Aramaic-speaking Christians from their towns in northern Iraq
Phrygia enters military conflict with Assyria over the Neo-Hittite lands of central Anatolia.
An Assyrian inscription from the reign of Sargon of Assyria names Mita, suggesting Phrygia has offered its submission and struck a truce.
Shalmaneser III of Assyria sacks Arzashkun, royal city of King Arame
Argishti I founds the fortress of Erebuni, origin of Yerevan
Tiglath-pileser III defeats Sarduri II and his Syrian allies
Sargon II defeats Rusa I and sacks the temple of Haldi at Musasir
Cyrus the Great of Persia conquers Babylon and grants the Judaean exiles freedom to return to Zion
The Jewish Publication Society publishes its Tanakh, replacing its translation of 1917
Shortly after reaching Trapezus, the Ten Thousand decisively defeat the Colchians in battle.
Itamra the Sabaean sends gifts to Sargon II of Assyria
Aelius Gallus besieges Marib for six days and retreats
Cyaxares and Nabopolassar of Babylon destroy Nineveh
War with Lydia ends after the battle of the eclipse, fixing the Halys River frontier
Nabopolassar seizes Babylon and restores native Babylonian kingship
Babylonians and Medes sack Nineveh, the Assyrian capital
Crown prince Nebuchadnezzar II defeats Necho II's Egyptians at Carchemish
Nebuchadnezzar captures Jerusalem and deports King Jehoiachin
Nebuchadnezzar II dies; four kings follow in six years
Cyrus the Great wins at Opis and Babylon falls without real resistance
Nebuchadnezzar is first attested as high priest of the Eanna temple in Uruk, a post he is recorded in until 617 BCE
He commands the Babylonian army at Carchemish and defeats the Egyptians under Necho II; on his father's death he returns to Babylon and is proclaimed king
He invades Egypt; the Babylonian Chronicle records heavy losses on both sides and the invasion fails
He takes Jerusalem, captures King Jeconiah and installs Zedekiah as king of Judah
After Zedekiah's revolt he destroys Jerusalem and the Kingdom of Judah, and the Jews are deported to Babylonia
The land city of Tyre is taken after a siege, while the island part of the city is left alone
A fragmentary inscription suggests a further campaign against Egypt under Amasis II, which did not bring Egypt under Babylonian rule
Nebuchadnezzar dies at Babylon after a reign of 43 years and Amel-Marduk succeeds him
He succeeds his father as king, still under Median overlordship
After at least three years of hostilities he captures Ecbatana and overthrows the Median kingdom
He defeats Croesus, occupies Sardis and conquers the Lydian kingdom
His army routs the Babylonians at Opis and he enters Babylon
He crosses the Hindu Kush and collects tribute from the Indus cities
He dies around December and is succeeded by his son Cambyses II
Claudius Rich's topographical records of the ruins of Babylon, the first ever published, appeared
Robert Koldewey began his part in the excavation of Babylon
The excavation, which had uncovered 14 metres of the gate's foundation, came to an end
After the First World War ended, the smaller frontal gate was reconstructed in the Pergamon Museum in Berlin
A smaller reproduction of the gate, built under Saddam Hussein, was completed in Iraq
The government of Iraq petitioned Germany to return the gate, and petitioned again in 2009
Cyrus II defeats Astyages and takes over the Median Empire
Cyrus defeats the Babylonians at Opis and enters Babylon
Cambyses II defeats Psamtik III at Pelusium and conquers Egypt
Xerxes invades Greece, wins at Thermopylae, sacks Athens but loses at Salamis
Egypt revolts on the death of Darius II and stays independent for six decades
Alexander the Great defeats Darius III at Gaugamela
Alexander burns Persepolis; Darius III is murdered by his satrap Bessus
With six nobles he kills Gaumata at the fortress of Sikayauvati and takes the throne, then faces revolts in most parts of the empire
He campaigns in Central Asia, Aria and Bactria and winters in Gandhara before conquering the lands around the Indus River in 515 BCE
He crosses the Bosphorus on a bridge of boats and invades European Scythia, where the Scythians avoid battle
He travels to Egypt for the opening of the canal linking the Nile to the Red Sea
The Persian army sent against Athens and Eretria is defeated at the Battle of Marathon
Darius dies after a revolt in Egypt delays his planned expedition; Xerxes succeeds him
Cyrus conquered Babylon, after which the Cylinder was made and buried as a foundation deposit
Hormuzd Rassam found the Cylinder at Babylon, and Henry Rawlinson announced it to the Royal Asiatic Society in November
J. B. Nies of Yale University published the text of the smaller fragment, B
Fragment A was restored, re-fired and given plaster fillings
The Cylinder was displayed in Tehran for the celebration of 2,500 years of Persian monarchy
Fragments A and B were reunited at the British Museum
Two clay fragments in the museum since 1881 were identified as part of a tablet bearing the same text, and the Cylinder was lent again to Iran
Darius was crowned king of the Achaemenid Empire in the summer, and the rebellions that the inscription describes followed the death of Cambyses II
Darius fought nineteen battles in a period of one year, ending in December, to put down the rebellions
Robert Sherley saw the inscription on a diplomatic mission to Safavid Persia and brought it to the attention of Western European scholars
Pietro della Valle visited the inscription and made preliminary drawings
Henry Rawlinson began studying the inscription in earnest and later scaled the cliff to copy the Old Persian text
Rawlinson sent a full and accurate copy of the Old Persian inscription to Europe
The site became a UNESCO World Heritage Site
The fall of the Sasanian empire to the Arab conquerors makes Arabic the language of government
Death of the poet Rumi, author of the Masnavi
The Mughal emperor Akbar makes Persian the language of all government records in his empire
Persian is replaced by English and local languages as the official language of British India
Date of the earliest remains and of the coin hoard laid under the foundation boxes of the Apadana
Darius I dies, and Xerxes I completes the Tachara palace
Alexander the Great takes Persepolis, and a fire destroys its palaces
Persepolis is still the capital of Persia as a province of the Macedonian Empire
The Sasanian prince Shapur Sakanshah leaves an inscription naming the site Sad-stun
García de Silva Figueroa links Chehel Minar with the Persepolis of the classical authors
Ernst Herzfeld and Erich Schmidt begin the first scientific excavations
Pepin the Short grants the pope former Byzantine lands in Italy, founding the Papal States
Güshi Khan confers authority over Tibet on the Fifth Dalai Lama, founding the Ganden Phodrang government
Italian troops take Rome on 20 September, ending the Papal States
The Lateran Treaty creates Vatican City, where the pope holds all legislative, executive and judicial power
After the Tibetan uprising the 14th Dalai Lama flees to India, and the Lhasa government is dissolved
A revolution and a new constitution make Iran an Islamic Republic headed by a senior Shia jurist
A Persian army under Xerxes defeats the Greeks at Thermopylae and Artemisium, and the Greek navy wins at Salamis
A delegation from Samos tells the Greeks that the Ionian cities are ready to revolt, and the fleet sails for Samos
The Greeks land, defeat the Persian force and burn its ships
Nabataea was annexed by the Romans and became part of the province of Arabia Petraea
An earthquake destroyed many buildings and crippled the water management system
The Urn Tomb was consecrated as a church in the time of Bishop Jason
The Swiss traveller Johann Ludwig Burckhardt became the first European to describe the ruins
Petra was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site
Philip II wins at Chaeronea and forms the Hellenic League to make war on Persia, while Artaxerxes III is murdered
A Macedonian expeditionary corps lands in Asia Minor, Philip is murdered and Alexander III and Darius III take their thrones
Memnon of Rhodes defeats a Macedonian force and most Greek cities return to Persian control
Alexander defeats the Persian satraps' army at the Granicus
Dascylium, Sardis and Ephesus fall to Alexander or are evacuated by their garrisons
Alexander besieges Miletus, which resists him
Alexander crosses into Asia and defeats the Persian satraps at the Battle of the Granicus
Alexander occupies most of Asia Minor, taking coastal settlements such as Miletus and Halicarnassus
Darius marches north around the mountains, captures Issus and cuts Alexander's supply lines
Alexander's army defeats the Persians on the Pinarus and Darius flees
The Spartan king Agis III defeats the Macedonian general Coragus in the Peloponnese
Agis is finally defeated at the Battle of Megalopolis
Darius III loses the Battle of Issus to Alexander, who captures his wife, mother and two daughters
Alexander takes Tyre after a siege from January to July and then Gaza, and Egypt surrenders to him
Darius makes a third offer of terms, which Alexander refuses
Alexander marches from Egypt through Syria, crosses the Euphrates and then the Tigris
The armies meet at Gaugamela and Alexander leads a wedge into the Persian centre
Darius flees and Babylon is surrendered to Alexander
Seleucus retakes Babylon after the Battle of Gaza, the starting point of the Seleucid era
Seleucus and Lysimachus defeat and kill Antigonus at the Battle of Ipsus
Seleucus defeats Lysimachus at Corupedium but is assassinated within months
Antiochus III begins a seven-year eastern campaign that earns him the title 'the Great'
Rome routs Antiochus III's army at the Battle of Magnesia
Antiochus IV's suppression of Jewish practice sparks the Maccabean revolt
Mithridates I of Parthia conquers Mesopotamia and captures Seleucia-on-Tigris
Pompey deposes Antiochus XIII and makes Syria a Roman province
Pompey invades Iberia and forces King Artoces to submit
Pharasmanes I seizes Armenia for his brother Mithridates
Vespasian fortifies Mtskheta for King Mithridates of Iberia
Vakhtang I Gorgasali joins the Armenian revolt against Persia
After the Battle of Ancyra, Antioch becomes the main centre of the Seleucid Empire
Antioch passes with Syria to the Roman Republic
A huge earthquake strikes while Trajan is in the city
Khosrow I destroys Antioch and deports its people to Persian Mesopotamia
Byzantine forces capture the city after a siege
The Crusaders take Antioch after a siege of eight months
Baybars captures and razes the city
Mithridates I Ktistes takes the title of king
Pharnaces I captures Sinope and makes it his capital
Mithridates VI overruns Roman Asia and orders the massacre of Romans and Italians
Peace of Dardanus ends the First Mithridatic War
Pompey routs Mithridates on the Lycus river
Mithridates VI dies at Panticapaeum; Pompey divides Pontus
Bedouin shepherds found the first seven scrolls in jars in what became Cave 1, between November 1946 and February 1947
Millar Burrows of the American Schools of Oriental Research announced the discovery
Cave 4, by far the most productive of the caves, was found and excavated
Four scrolls advertised in The Wall Street Journal were bought for Israel for $250,000
Cave 11 yielded the last fragments found near Qumran, among them the Temple Scroll
The collection moved to the newly built Shrine of the Book in Jerusalem
A Facsimile Edition and the opening of the Huntington Library's photographs ended restricted access
The 40th and final volume of Discoveries in the Judaean Desert was published
The Fourth Syrian War begins between Ptolemaic Egypt under Ptolemy IV and the Seleucid Empire under Antiochus III
Both armies are on campaign through Syria and meet near the town of Rafah
Theodotus the Aetolian enters the Ptolemaic camp to kill Ptolemy but finds the king's tent empty
After five days of skirmishing the two armies are drawn up and the battle is fought
Priests meet at Memphis to give thanks for the victory, and a stele honours Ptolemy as pharaoh in Greek as well as Egyptian
Upper Egypt secedes under the pharaohs Hugronaphor and Ankhmakis, a separate kingdom lasting nearly twenty years
Antiochus defeats the army of Ptolemy V Epiphanes at Panium and recaptures Coele-Syria and Judea
Antiochus meets Roman envoys at Lysimachia, who demand that he leave Europe and restore the autonomy of the Greek cities of Asia Minor
Antiochus lands in Greece at Demetrias at the urging of the Aetolians, and Rome declares war in November
The Romans defeat Antiochus at Thermopylae and, in September, his fleet at Corycus
A combined Roman and Rhodian fleet defeats the Seleucid fleet at Myonessus, opening the way to Asia Minor
A truce is signed at Sardes
The Romans begin the Galatian War, and peace talks are held with the Senate
The Treaty of Apamea is signed
The Seleucids are defeated by Rome at the Battle of Magnesia; in the same year Artaxias I founds a Hellenistic Armenian state, with Zariadres ruling the kingdom of Sophene.
Artaxias I's reign begins; he seizes Yervandashat and unites the Armenian Highlands at the expense of neighbouring tribes.
Artaxias founds Artaxata (Artashat) near the Araxes, at the junction of trade routes linking the Greek world with Bactria, India and the Black Sea.
Tigranes the Great enters Syria and establishes himself as its ruler, ending the Seleucid Empire in all but name.
Rome conquers Tigranes' empire; Armenia's brief imperial period ends.
After Pompey defeats Mithridates VI of Pontus at the Battle of the Lycus, Armenia becomes a Roman client kingdom.
Mark Antony invades and defeats the kingdom; Rome loses its hegemony in the Final War of the Republic of 32–30 BCE.
The last Artaxiad kings are overthrown, suspected of allegiance to Parthia.
The emperor Trajan captures Ctesiphon, and Hadrian returns it in 117
Septimius Severus sacks the city and sells thousands of its people into slavery
The Sasanians hold Ctesiphon and make it their capital
After the conquest of Antioch, Khosrow I builds a new city near Ctesiphon for the people he captured
Yusuf As'ar Yath'ar besieges Najran, where many Christians are killed
Kaleb of Aksum invades, and Yusuf is defeated and killed
Albanians join the Armenian rising crushed at the Battle of Avarayr
Crassus, Pompey and Caesar renew their alliance at Ravenna and Luca, and Crassus arranges to have Syria as his province
Crassus invades the Parthian client-state of Osroene while Surena defeats and executes Mithridates IV at Seleucia
In the spring Crassus rejects Armenia's offer and marches through Mesopotamia
Surena's horse archers and cataphracts defeat the Romans near Carrhae, and Publius Crassus dies with his force
Crassus is killed at a truce meeting, and Cassius leads about 10,000 survivors back to Syria
A Parthian invasion is stopped and repulsed by Publius Ventidius Bassus
Mark Antony invades Parthia in the Atropatene campaign, which also fails
She stands near the cross at the crucifixion of Jesus, in John's account
The Council of Ephesus declares her Theotokos, the God-bearer
Pope Pius IX proclaims the Immaculate Conception
Pope Pius XII defines the Assumption in Munificentissimus Deus
He travels to Jerusalem for Passover, enters the city and drives the money changers from the Temple
After a last meal with his twelve apostles he is arrested, brought before Caiaphas and the Sanhedrin and handed to Pilate
He is crucified, with Pilate's inscription reading King of the Jews; the date is 30 or 33 CE
His followers report his empty tomb and appearances, and the Acts of the Apostles places his ascension forty days later
At the Council of Jerusalem Peter, James and John accept his mission to the gentiles
He goes to Jerusalem with a collection of money and is arrested in the Temple
Constantine and Licinius grant Christians freedom of worship, the so-called Edict of Milan
The Council of Nicaea, called by Constantine, defines the faith in the Nicene Creed
Theodosius I makes Nicene Christianity the religion of the Roman Empire
The Great Schism divides the Latin West from the Greek East
Martin Luther’s Ninety-five Theses begin the Protestant Reformation
Athanasius gives the list of the 27 books in his Easter letter and calls them canonised
The Council of Carthage accepts a summary of the lost acts of the Synod of Hippo Regius of 393
Martin Luther's translation of the New Testament appears
The Authorized Version, also called the King James Version, is published
The destruction of the Second Temple, from which Talmudic tradition is dated as emerging
Ravina II, by medieval chronicles' reckoning, dies, and the Talmud is said to have stopped
The Disputation of Paris examines charges against the Talmud brought by Nicholas Donin
Daniel Bomberg begins printing the first complete Babylonian Talmud at Venice
Menachem Romm of Vilna prints the edition on which most later ones are modelled
Mani is born in Mesopotamia, near the Persian capital Ctesiphon
The Tang emperor Wuzong bans Manichaeism in China
The image of Mani as the Buddha of Light is carved at Cao’an near Quanzhou
